title: How to Structure a Real Estate Joint Venture Agreement (Step-by-Step Guide)

sections.content: Two investors. One deal. Unlimited potential — or a complete disaster. Which outcome you get often comes down to one thing: whether you took the time to properly structure a real estate joint venture agreement before the first dollar changed hands. A joint venture (JV) lets you combine your strengths with a partner's resources, but without a clear written agreement, even the best deals can fall apart fast. This guide walks you through every key piece of a solid JV agreement so you can partner up with confidence.
What Is a Real Estate Joint Venture Agreement?

A real estate joint venture agreement is a legal contract between two or more parties who agree to work together on a specific real estate project. Unlike a general partnership, a JV is typically deal-specific. Once the project is complete — whether that's a fix-and-flip, a wholesale assignment, or a rental acquisition — the partnership ends. Each party brings something different to the table: one might bring capital while the other brings deal-finding expertise, local market knowledge, or construction management skills. The agreement spells out exactly who contributes what and who gets paid what in return. If you're new to real estate investing, check out our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide before diving into your first JV deal.
Why You Absolutely Need a Written Agreement

Handshake deals feel good in the moment. They fall apart when the rehab runs $30,000 over budget or the property sits on the market for four months longer than expected. A written joint venture agreement creates a shared rulebook that both parties agreed to when everyone was calm and optimistic. It defines what happens when things go right — and when they go wrong. Courts also take written contracts seriously. A verbal agreement is nearly impossible to enforce, and in real estate deals that often involve six-figure sums, that risk is simply not worth taking.
In real estate partnerships, the time you spend negotiating the agreement upfront is the cheapest legal protection you will ever buy. Every hour spent now saves ten hours in court later.
The 7 Core Components of a Strong JV Agreement
1. Identify the Parties and the Purpose

Start with the basics. List the full legal names of all parties involved — individuals, LLCs, or corporations — and define the specific project. Do not make this vague. Instead of writing 'fix-and-flip properties in Texas,' write '123 Oak Street, Dallas, TX 75201 — acquisition, renovation, and resale.' Deal-specific language protects everyone and limits the scope of the partnership. If you're working in active markets like [Dallas, TX](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) or [Atlanta, GA](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), being precise about property address and deal type is especially important given how fast inventory moves.
2. Define Each Partner's Contributions

List exactly what each party is bringing to the deal. Contributions fall into a few categories: capital (cash for purchase and rehab), sweat equity (finding the deal, managing contractors, handling closings), expertise (market knowledge, relationships, licensing), and credit (if one partner is qualifying for financing). Be specific with dollar amounts and time commitments. For example: 'Partner A will contribute $85,000 in acquisition and renovation capital. Partner B will source the deal, manage the renovation, and oversee the sale at no additional charge to the JV.'
3. Set the Profit Split and Return of Capital

This is usually where JV conversations get the most heated — and where the most mistakes happen. A common structure returns the capital partner's investment first before any profit is split. From there, profits are divided according to what each party contributed. A typical split for a deal where one partner funds everything and the other manages the deal might be 50/50 after capital return. But there is no universal rule. A money partner taking all the risk might negotiate 60/40 or even 70/30 in their favor. Whatever you agree on, write it down with exact percentages and a clear order of operations for how money flows out at closing.

Before agreeing to any profit split, run the numbers on your deal using the free [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator). Knowing your projected profit, repair costs, and ARV makes it much easier to negotiate a split that's fair to both partners.
4. Assign Decision-Making Roles and Voting Rights

Who has the final say on renovation decisions? What if one partner wants to list at $285,000 and the other insists on $310,000? Your agreement should define who manages day-to-day operations and what decisions require unanimous consent. A simple structure is to designate one 'managing partner' who handles operations and a 'capital partner' who must approve any decisions that affect the budget by more than a set threshold — say, $5,000 or more. This keeps things moving without leaving the money partner out of the loop on major choices.
5. Set a Timeline and Milestones

Vague timelines create friction. Your agreement should include an expected close date for acquisition, a renovation completion date, a target list date, and a final sale deadline. Include language about what happens if these milestones are missed. For instance: 'If the property has not sold within 120 days of listing, both partners will agree to a price reduction of no less than 3% every 30 days thereafter.' This kind of language removes emotion from hard decisions down the road.
6. Address Disputes and Default

Even great partnerships hit bumps. Your agreement should outline a dispute resolution process — typically starting with direct negotiation, then mediation, and only then arbitration or litigation. It should also define what constitutes a default (for example, a capital partner failing to fund within 10 business days of a draw request) and what remedies are available. Stating these terms upfront keeps minor disagreements from turning into expensive legal battles.
7. Define the Exit Strategy

Every JV needs a clear exit. For a fix-and-flip, that's straightforward: sell the property and split proceeds. For a rental acquisition, it gets more complex. What if one partner wants to sell after two years and the other wants to hold for five? Include a buyout clause that gives one partner the right to purchase the other's interest at fair market value, along with a timeline and valuation method. Markets like [Phoenix, AZ](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) have seen rapid appreciation in recent years, making buyout terms especially important for rental JVs in high-growth areas.
Common JV Structures in Real Estate

items: Money Partner + Deal Finder: One partner funds, one sources and manages. Profits typically split 50/50 after capital return.
Active + Passive: One partner handles all operations; the other is a silent investor seeking a preferred return (e.g., 8% annually) plus a share of upside.
Skill + Skill: Two operators each bring different expertise — one handles acquisitions, the other handles construction. Capital is split equally and so are profits.
Experienced + Inexperienced: A veteran investor mentors a newer one in exchange for a larger profit share — often 60/40 or 70/30 in the experienced partner's favor.
Local Market Expert + Out-of-State Capital: Common in hot markets where out-of-state investors want exposure but need boots on the ground.

sections.content: Do You Need a Real Estate Attorney?

Short answer: yes, for any deal above $50,000. Templates you find online can serve as a starting point, but a real estate attorney familiar with your state's laws will catch issues a generic document misses — especially around entity structure, liability, and tax treatment. If you and your partner are using LLCs (which is strongly recommended), the attorney can also help structure operating agreements that align with your JV terms. The cost is usually $500 to $1,500 for a well-drafted agreement, which is a rounding error on most deals. If you're just getting started with partnerships and want to understand the deal side more deeply first, our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) guide covers how to find and evaluate deals before bringing in a partner.

Always run your JV deal through a numbers analysis before approaching a partner. Investors take you more seriously — and you negotiate better terms — when you show up with actual data: ARV, repair estimate, projected profit, and return timeline. Preparation signals professionalism.
Quick Checklist Before You Sign

items: Full legal names and entity types for all parties are listed
Specific property address and deal scope are defined
Each partner's contributions are itemized in writing
Profit split percentage and order of distributions are clearly stated
Managing partner and decision-making thresholds are defined
Timeline and key milestones are included
Exit strategy and buyout terms are included
Agreement has been reviewed by a licensed real estate attorney
